gateway.text:
DNA repair is the cell’s system for finding and fixing damage in DNA—the molecule that stores genetic instructions. Different problems use different repair routes: a damaged DNA “letter” may be replaced, a bulky distortion may be cut out, or a break in both strands may be repaired by using a matching template or by joining the ends.

DNA damage response (DDR) is the larger coordination system. It detects the problem, sends signals, pauses the cell cycle, and helps decide what happens next. Importantly, a warning signal does not prove the damage was successfully repaired; the cell may instead tolerate the damage, stop dividing, or die. [DNA damage and repair](/education/concepts/cancer-biology/genome-instability-and-repair/dna-damage-and-repair-overview/#how-it-works)

[[visual:1]]

In this cartoon, PARP first responds to DNA damage. It can then become a physical obstacle at a DNA-copying fork; repairing the resulting damage and removing the trapped obstacle are separate tasks. [PARP trapping and recycling](/education/guides/from-variant-to-drug/04-parp-trapping-and-recycling/#the-repair-worker-can-become-an-obstacle)

Would you like a cartoon explanation of **PARP trapping** or **BRCA-related repair** next?
